what: Where the Toyota row of the carmaker table links
was: Toyota’s RAV4 manual was linked at assets.sia.toyota.com. That address now refuses every request, so only the archived copy next to it would open.
now: The row points at assets.sipb.toyota.com, the address Toyota’s own 2025 RAV4 manuals page uses today, and its read date is Nov 12, 2026. The archived copy is still linked beside it.
why: Toyota moved its manual files. The PDF at the new address has the same SHA-256 as the copy we quoted on Nov 3, so the RAV4 advice, a technician check for any tire over 6 years old, has not changed.

what: How many Kirkland Signature medicines the Perrigo page credits to Perrigo
was: The page and its description said FDA files tie Perrigo to 38 Kirkland Signature medicines, 20 of them through an FDA approval Perrigo holds, and the table was titled as 38 Kirkland products.
now: The page says 25 Kirkland Signature medicines, 13 of them through an FDA approval Perrigo holds. The table, which also lists Member’s Mark medicines, is titled as 38 Kirkland Signature and Member’s Mark products.
why: When Member’s Mark medicines were added to Perrigo’s record, the count on the page took them in too, though the sentence names only Kirkland Signature.

what: How many Kirkland Signature medicines the LNK International page credits to LNK
was: The page and its description said LNK makes 13 Kirkland Signature medicines, and the table was titled as 13 Kirkland products.
now: The page says eight Kirkland Signature medicines. The table, which also lists five Member’s Mark medicines, is titled as 13 Kirkland Signature and Member’s Mark products.
why: When Member’s Mark medicines were added to LNK’s record, the count on the page took them in too, though the sentence names only Kirkland Signature.

what: The year of the consultant's dishwasher life study
was: The chart of DOE's dishwasher estimates called the 12.6-year figure a 2016 consultant's study.
now: It is Navigant's 2010 study for ACEEE, as DOE's 2022 technical support document says.
why: Re-reading AHAM's comment in DOE's support document for the dishwasher page showed the study date we had printed was wrong.

what: Brands the decoder reads
was: The decoder didn't read Hisense or Sub-Zero, read every Kenmore serial in Whirlpool's layout, and cited one Viking recall notice (dishwashers, 2015).
now: Hisense fridge serials starting C and a year are read as the build date (Recall record, from Hisense's 2022 recall). Sub-Zero points to the Date Code printed on its tag, from Sub-Zero's support page. Kenmore serials starting with a digit are read in LG's layout, still Unconfirmed, as CPSC notices show LG built Kenmore fridges with model numbers starting 795. Viking also cites its 2009 and 2013 fridge recall notices.
why: While building the fridge and freezer page we read every household fridge and freezer recall in CPSC's database and the Hisense and Sub-Zero pages.

what: How sure we are of the Bosch FD date rule
was: Bosch was marked Reported: the FD rule came only from two how-to guides, Hunker and ServiceMag, neither of which cites Bosch.
now: Bosch is marked Recall record. Two CPSC recall notices issued with Bosch's maker BSH give build dates that fit the rule: dishwashers manufactured from January 2008 through December 2013 carry FD 8801 to FD 9312 (2015), and May 1999 to July 2005 runs from FD 7905 to FD 8507 (2009). Viking joins the decoder on the same footing, from its 2015 recall notice.
why: While building the dishwasher page we read every CPSC dishwasher recall; the BSH notices pair FD ranges with build dates.

what: Is Kirkland vodka Grey Goose?
was: “No record we found says so”, with the two French vodka approvals held by MISA Imports, which name no distillery.
now: No. Grey Goose’s own FAQ calls the claim “completely false” and says Grey Goose “does not produce nor privately label Kirkland vodka”. The MISA approvals are still there, and still name no distillery.
why: We hadn’t used Grey Goose’s own answer to the question, which is a stronger record than finding nothing.

what: What is free to use, in the terms
was: “Use the site and the tire lookup free, as often as you like, with no sign-up.”
now: “Use the site and its lookups free, as often as you like, with no sign-up.”
why: The site now has four lookups: tire DOT codes, tire age, battery date codes and USDA plant numbers. Naming only the tire lookup read as if the other three weren’t covered.

what: What the 2012 safety sheets prove, on the Sun Products page
was: The scale on the page set Confirmed at a company or Costco speaking for itself. Costco published the sheets that name Sun Products, so that tie could look Confirmed.
now: A safety sheet names the supplier responsible, which How we know counts as Documented. Confirmed would need a code on the pack that leads to a plant, and these sheets give only Sun’s head office in Wilton, Connecticut.
why: A safety sheet comes from the supplier, which the old wording made look like the company speaking for itself. Our stamp rules count it as a record, so Documented is the top step it can reach.

what: Links on eight source cards
was: The cards for The Costco Connection, Kia’s investor pages and newsroom, Georgia’s governor, Hip2Save, Slickdeals, Krazy Coupon Lady and ACDelco Canada linked pages that had moved or no longer exist.
now: Costco’s magazine now lives at costcoconnection.com, where Costco’s old address sends you. Kia, Georgia, Hip2Save and Slickdeals link their pages’ new addresses. Krazy Coupon Lady and ACDelco Canada have no terms page any more, so their cards link the privacy policy and home page and say so.
why: The sites moved or removed those pages. A link check in our site audit found them; no answer depended on the old addresses.

what: The Sources page’s summary in search results
was: “The government records behind every answer on Who Actually Makes…”
now: “Every source behind our answers, from government registers to company filings and press reports…”
why: Only 24 of the 137 sources are government registers or regulators. The rest include makers’ own words, retailers and press reports, and the page says which is which.

what: How strong each SM Global tie is
was: The three golf ball ties and the driver tie showed their stamps without saying which USGA list each comes from.
now: A new table puts all four at Documented and names the record behind each: the current USGA conforming ball list for the Performance+ and Tour Performance balls, a past edition for the 2017 Performance One, and the driver head list for the driver.
why: The driver and the balls stand on different USGA lists, and the 2017 ball only on an old edition; the table now shows which is which.

what: Which Kirkland tequila approvals Sazerac North America holds
was: One approval: the 2020 Kirkland Signature Tequila Blanco, held by Sazerac North America as importer.
now: Approvals from 2017, 2018 and November 2020, held by Sazerac North America as importer, with Wide World Importers (later World Wide Importers) as the name on the label. A table lists every Kirkland approval a Sazerac company holds, re-read each week.
why: We started reading every Kirkland label approval on TTB’s registry each week, and the 2017 and 2018 approvals were among those we hadn’t read.

what: How strong each Sazerac tie is
was: The vodka, bourbon and tequila ties were stamped, with their TTB approvals only in the evidence list.
now: A new table shows all four at Documented, each from a TTB label approval: tequila from August 2017, bourbon from December 2020 and May 2026, and the American Vodka from July 2026.
why: A label approval names who filed it. The table makes clear that is the record behind each Sazerac tie, not a code on the bottle leading to a distillery.

what: How strong each Saturn Petcare tie is
was: The wet cat and wet dog food ties showed their stamps without the record named next to them.
now: A new table places both at Documented, each from North Dakota's pet food register, renewed December 2025, where the registrations are filed care of Saturn Petcare.
why: Saturn's tie comes from a single state register and no other record, which readers judging it should see in one line.

what: The privacy policy’s summary in search results
was: “No cookies for visitors, no ads, no accounts.”
now: “No ads, accounts or forms. Google Analytics cookies only outside the EU, UK and Switzerland.”
why: Google Analytics sets two cookies for visitors outside those places. The policy itself always said so; only the summary shown in search contradicted it.

what: What Google Analytics counts, in the privacy policy
was: The Google Analytics row listed pages viewed, how you arrived, time on the page, and your general area and device type.
now: It also lists which links you click in the box of other answers at the foot of a page. A new line says the tire age checker and the battery date code decoder work out the answer on your device and send the code nowhere.
why: Since Nov 5 Google Analytics has counted those clicks, under the same rules as page views, and the policy didn’t say so. We missed it when the box was added.

what: How strong each Perrigo tie is
was: The 26 medicine ties sat in a folded list, each stamped, with no summary of the records they rest on.
now: A new table groups them so the scale stays short: the medicines named on both DailyMed labels and Drugs@FDA in one row, and the January 2022 Aller-Fex recall, from FDA recall reports, in another. All are Documented, and each tie is still listed one by one below.
why: With 26 ties, one row each would have repeated the same step and records two dozen times; grouping shows at a glance that every Perrigo tie stands on FDA records.

what: How the Perrigo page says the company is tied to Kirkland
was: The page led with one record, Perrigo packaging Kirkland Aller-Fex in a 2022 recall, and said “Only the Aller-Fex recall names Perrigo so far.”
now: The page leads with FDA’s own files, which tie Perrigo to 25 Kirkland Signature medicines; for 13 of them a Perrigo company holds the approval number printed on the Kirkland label. A table lists each one with its FDA number, and the Aller-Fex recall is the first of them.
why: Our Nov 5 read of Kirkland labels on DailyMed, checked against Drugs@FDA, added the other ties to our records and to the medicine page, but this page’s wording wasn’t rewritten, so it contradicted its own list of answers for three days.

what: What MISA’s label approvals prove, on the MISA Imports page
was: Confirmed, by the page’s scale, meant the company or Costco saying so in its own words. MISA files its own label approvals with TTB, so those could read as Confirmed.
now: A TTB label approval is a public record naming MISA as importer: Documented, by the rules on How we know. Confirmed would need a code on the bottle that leads to a factory, and the tequila’s NOM number leads to the distillery, not to MISA.
why: An importer’s own filing is easy to mistake for the importer vouching for the maker. The scale’s old wording invited that reading, which our stamp rules don’t allow.

what: How the Kimberly-Clark page explains the strength of each tie
was: Its strength scale put Confirmed at the company or Costco saying so in its own words, which read as if a statement from Kimberly-Clark would lift the facial tissue tie above the FSC code on the box.
now: It now follows How we know: Confirmed needs a code on the product that leads to a factory. The FSC code leads to Kimberly-Clark’s certificate, not a mill, so the tissue stays Documented and the diapers stay Reported. No stamp changed.
why: The scale was written for the four company pages published that day and didn’t follow our published stamp rules; on this page it muddied why a certificate code on the box isn’t a factory.

what: The “Next check” date on the company pages
was: Every company page said “Next check Nov 9”. Next week it would have said Nov 16, and so on, but no job was reading the registers and recalls behind these pages; the last read was Nov 3.
now: A job on our server re-reads North Dakota’s pet food register and FDA’s recall records for every company each month. Each page shows the date of that next read, Dec 3, or sooner where one of its answers falls due first, as on the Perrigo page.
why: Our schedule assumed a weekly script would run the re-read, and kept promising next Monday for it, but no script was set up to run it.

what: How many Kirkland medicines the LNK International page credits to LNK
was: The page said LNK is named as the maker of one Kirkland product, Severe Cold & Flu Plus Congestion, in FDA’s December 2024 recall, and that no other Kirkland medicine names LNK in a record we’d read.
now: The page says LNK makes eight Kirkland medicines, among them pain relievers, low-dose aspirin, a sleep aid and an allergy tablet. Some labels print “Manufactured by: LNK International, Inc.”; on others the label file lists LNK as the manufacturing establishment. The recall is one record among them.
why: The label files we read on Nov 5 name LNK on seven more Kirkland medicines. They reached our records but not this page’s wording.

what: How strong each LNK International tie is
was: Eight medicine ties were listed one by one, with their stamps but without the record kinds side by side.
now: A new table shows all eight at Documented and names what lies behind each: DailyMed labels for most, Drugs@FDA as well for the ibuprofen and sleep aid, and FDA recall reports for the December 2024 cold and flu recall.
why: Some LNK ties rest on a label alone and some on a label plus an FDA approval record, a difference the old layout hid.

what: How strong the Kruger Products tie is
was: The Ultra Soft Bath Tissue tie showed only its stamp.
now: A new table places it at Documented, from the FSC code on Costco's listing for the 231-sheet roll and Kruger's FSC certificate. The certificate lists ten sites, so no single mill is named.
why: Kruger is a Canadian company and its one US site is in Memphis; readers can now see the tie rests on a certificate code rather than a statement about where a roll was made.

what: How strong each Highline Warren tie is
was: Both motor oil ties carried their stamps, with the API directory and the Costco listing only in the evidence list further down.
now: A new table names, beside each tie, the API engine oil license directory, plus the Costco listing for the passenger-car oil, and puts both at Documented. The diesel 15W-40 tie rests on the API directory alone.
why: An API license names the company that answers for the oil, not the plant that blended it, so the table shows which record each oil's tie comes from and why neither goes higher.

what: What the record shows, on the Kirkland driver
was: The note under the driver said “The USGA and R&A list of conforming golf balls names this company as the ball’s manufacturer.”
now: Golf’s rule-makers, the USGA and The R&A, name SM Global as the manufacturer on their conforming list, the list of driver heads for this club. The list doesn’t say which factory made it, or where.
why: The note was written for the golf ball page and reused on the driver without being changed. The record, the company and the stamp were right.

what: How strong the Georgia-Pacific tie is
was: The 380-sheet bath tissue tie showed its stamp without naming the records it rests on.
now: A new table shows it at step three of four: the FSC code on the Costco listing, read against the FSC register and FSC's own label rules. It names no mill.
why: Georgia-Pacific has many mills, so readers wanted to know why the code on the pack lifts the tie to Documented and no higher.

what: What we accept as proof, on For makers and brands
was: “No photos and no private documents. We don’t buy products or photograph them.”
now: “No photos as proof, and no private documents.” It adds that a few tool pages show a licensed photo of where a code sits on a product, with brand names blurred, and that it never proves an answer.
why: The battery date code and USDA number pages show licensed photos, so “no photos” wasn’t true as written. What counts as proof hasn’t changed.

what: How to send a legal notice, on For makers and brands
was: “Email the same address with “Legal” in the subject line.”
now: “Write to us through the contact page with “Legal” in the subject line”, linked to the legal part of the contact page.
why: The page shows no email address, so “the same address” left a brand’s lawyer with nowhere to write.

what: How strong each First Quality tie is
was: The diaper ties were listed with their stamps but with no plain account of the records under each.
now: A new table ranks them. The tie from the SFI code on the Costco listing, traced through the SFI register and First Quality's own pages, is Documented; Bloomberg's December 2024 report and Fortune's April 2025 retelling are marked as reports, and that tie stays Reported.
why: This page holds one tie of each kind for the same diapers, and the gap between a certificate code on the box and a news story is the point a reader most needs to see.

what: Two “archived copy” links in the First Quality evidence
was: The evidence for the Cuties FAQ page and for First Quality’s 2024 SFI certificate linked Internet Archive copies dated Nov 5, 2026.
now: Both links are gone. The Internet Archive has no copy of either page. We keep our own copy of each, with its SHA-256 fingerprint, and will link the Archive again once a save works.
why: The Archive’s save queue turned our requests away, so the copies were never made, and the links opened a “not archived” page. We hadn’t checked that the saves went through.

what: Why the Duracell tie is only Reported
was: The page’s strength scale defined Confirmed as the company or Costco saying so in its own words. That suggested Costco’s chief executive naming Duracell ought to be Confirmed.
now: Under the rules on How we know, even a direct statement from Costco would be Documented; Confirmed needs a code on the pack that leads to a plant. The tie stays Reported because the Duracell line is the reporter’s words, not Costco’s.
why: The scale didn’t follow our published stamp rules, and on this page it blurred why a 2016 TV report, retold many times since, still counts only as Reported.

what: How strong each Diamond Pet Foods tie is
was: The page listed Diamond's four ties to Kirkland dog and cat food, each with its stamp, but didn't say what kind of record stood behind each one.
now: A new table puts all four on our four-step scale. The two 2012 ties rest on FDA recall notices and the two current ones on North Dakota's pet food register, and every one is Documented.
why: Readers asking whether Diamond still makes the food need to see that today's tie comes from a renewed register entry, not from the old recall.

what: The data page’s title in search results
was: “Open Data: Free Tire Plant Code and Tire Age Datasets”
now: “Open Data: 14 Free Datasets Behind Every Answer”, with the number taken from the list of files.
why: The page started with tire files and now holds 14, most of them about store brands, so the title described a small part of it.

what: The note on the relation field of the Who makes what file
was: The note said the field holds one of five values: made-by, bottled-by, packed-by, imported-by or recalled-by.
now: The note lists all 13 values the file holds, among them approval-holder, licensed-to, listed-maker and fsc-label-holder. The list is now read from the file each time it’s built, so it can’t fall behind again.
why: As we added medicine, motor oil, golf and paper answers, the file gained eight kinds of tie the note never mentioned. Code that kept only the five listed values would have dropped those rows.

what: The search title of Costco diapers
was: The title said Kirkland diapers cost “From 13¢”, rounding up the lowest price.
now: The lowest Kirkland price on the page was 12.5¢ a diaper, so the title now says “Under 13¢”. A whole-cent price still reads “From”.
why: Rounding 12.5¢ up made the title name a lowest price that a cheaper size undercut. Found in our site audit.

what: The date of one Barton 1792 label approval for Kirkland bourbon
was: Our record dated TTB approval 20342001000264 to January 29, 2021, and called it approved.
now: The approval was issued December 8, 2020, and TTB now lists it as surrendered. January 29, 2021 is the date TTB's search shows as completed. Barton's three other Kirkland approvals are still approved, so the answer is unchanged.
why: We read the date from TTB's search results instead of box 19 of the approval. Found when we started reading every Kirkland approval weekly.

what: Motorcraft's date code, on the battery date code decoder
was: We said we found no rule from Ford or Motorcraft and showed one how-to article's rule as Reported.
now: Ford's distributor manual, on a page effective May 2005, shows a shipping date sticker on the side of the battery reading C-2 and 3-2. The decoder reads both forms as a Maker's rule, with the record's date.
why: We missed the manual on the first read; it sits in a warranty PDF, not a consumer page.

what: Kirkland Stool Softener, on the Kirkland medicine page
was: We said the label file named no company.
now: The label says “Distributed by: PL Developments”, so the table names PL Developments as the distributor. That doesn't show who made it. Labels that name no company go from 3 to 2.
why: We missed the line on the label when we read it, and found it on a re-read.

what: ACDelco's P series, on the battery date code decoder
was: We showed the P series as Reported, from a seller's guide.
now: ACDelco's warranty sheet, revised February 2015, says the first character is P or S and that P 094N means September 2014. P now reads as a Maker's rule, with the record's date.
why: We found ACDelco's own sheet on a later read.

what: Deka's letter date code, on the battery date code decoder
was: Reported: letter codes for Deka came only from a seller's guide, and the 3/23 ship sticker was the one format we could confirm.
now: Maker's rule: Deka's care sheet prints a Shipping Date Code, a month letter that skips I, then a year digit, with L1 as November 2011. The two-digit form such as D24 stays Reported.
why: We found Deka's own sheet the day the page went live, while reading its storage guidance.

what: Opening line of the store-brand motor oil answer
was: For eight others, including Kirkland, Amazon Basics, Meijer, Do It Best and Signature Select, most or all of the oils are licensed to one company: Highline Warren LLC.
now: For eight others, including Kirkland, Amazon Basics, Meijer, Do It Best and Signature Select, some or all of the oils are licensed to one company: Highline Warren LLC.
why: "Most or all" was too strong for every brand: one of the five Members Mark listings is on Highline Warren's license. The company, the license and the counts were right; the summary wording was not.

what: The stamps line under How to read this list
was: Every answer here but three is Documented. The exceptions are the original 2016 golf ball and the 2020 wedges and 2023 irons, marked Reported.
now: Five answers are Reported: the same three, plus the 48-count AA and AAA batteries. The count and names now come from the data, in a chart.
why: The two battery answers are stamped Reported in our records, and the typed line had not been updated for them. The stamps themselves did not change.

what: What the proof is, on How We Know
was: The proof is always a public record you can open yourself. Every answer rests on records anyone can open.
now: The proof is always something you can open yourself, and the stamp says how strong it is. A press report on its own can only earn a Reported stamp.
why: Some answers rest on press reports, stamped Reported, so not all proof is a public record.

what: Trust note on the homepage
was: Public records only. No rumors, no guesses, no photos as proof.
now: Records first. A press report only earns a Reported stamp and is never shown as fact.
why: The old wording didn't match the site: we use some press reports, stamped Reported, and we publish a page testing rumors.

what: Sources figure on the homepage
was: 82 public sources, all primary records
now: 82 sources, 64 of them primary records. Both figures now come from the sources file.
why: Not all our sources are primary records. Some are press reports or other secondary sources.

what: Kirkland product count on the homepage
was: 35 Kirkland products
now: 76 Kirkland products. The count now comes from the Kirkland data file.
why: The number was typed in by hand and fell behind as answers were added.

what: Opening line of the Kirkland medicine answer
was: We read 47 Costco labels on FDA’s DailyMed.
now: We read 47 Costco labels on DailyMed, the US government’s library of drug labels.
why: DailyMed is run by the National Library of Medicine, not FDA. The labels, the companies and the counts were right; the name of the publisher was not.

what: Who approves corrections, on How We Know and About
was: Jeremiah approves every Confirmed stamp, anything that alleges a safety or legal problem, and every correction.
now: Same, except corrections: only those that change a maker, a stamp or a named company need approval. Typo, count and broken-link fixes go live without waiting and are logged.
why: The page promised more than our practice since 5 November, when smaller fixes stopped waiting for approval. The page now says what we do.

what: Who makes Kirkland Signature dog food
was: The only public record we'd found was Diamond Pet Foods' 2012 recall notice, so we said we couldn't name who makes today's bags.
now: North Dakota's pet food register lists all 12 Kirkland dry dog formulas as Costco's, care of Diamond Pet, renewed December 2025. We added wet food (Saturn Petcare), biscuits (North River Enterprises), jerky (Phelps Industries) and dental chews (Nylabone) from the same register.
why: We hadn't searched North Dakota's pet food register before. It carries the 12 dry dog registrations Costco renewed in December 2025, each filed care of Diamond Pet, with the label files that go with them, which is a newer record than a 2012 recall.

what: The cold brew line under What we don’t know
was: The 2023 recall record covers only four lots, with best-by dates of October 19 to 22, 2023.
now: The 2023 recall record covers only the lots it lists: nine lots with best-by dates of October 19 to 27, 2023, 231,071 cases in all.
why: FDA’s record lists nine lots (231019 to 231027), not four. The company and the record were right; the lot count and date range were not.

what: Who makes Kirkland Signature cat food
was: The only public record we'd found was Diamond Pet Foods' 2012 recall notice; we hadn't found who makes the wet cat food.
now: North Dakota's pet food register lists the three Kirkland dry cat formulas care of Diamond Pet and the four pate cat foods care of Saturn Petcare, all renewed December 2025.
why: The same register search turned up the cat registrations. Besides the dry formulas filed care of Diamond Pet, it gave us a named company for the wet pate for the first time: Saturn Petcare, which no record we'd read before had tied to Kirkland.

what: Opening line of the bourbon answer
was: Two companies hold US label approvals for Kirkland Signature bourbon.
now: Three companies hold US label approvals for Kirkland Signature bourbon.
why: The paragraph went on to name three approval holders: Barton 1792 Distillery, Buffalo Trace Distillery, Inc. and Tennessee Distilling Group. The count was wrong; the companies and records were not.
